## Introduction {#slide-2}

Statistical Inference is making a conclusion about population parameters based on sample statistics.

Two main types of statistical inference are estimating parameters (Chapter 9) and testing claims about parameters (Chapter 10) using statistics.

## Estimation examples {#slide-3}

Estimate the  mean  annual loss from damage in the entire population of millions of apartment owners.

Estimate the true (or population)  proportion  of young adult internet users who use social-networking sites.

Estimate the true (or population)  variance  of service lives of hearing aid batteries of a specific type.

## Methods of estimation {#slide-5}

A  point estimate  of a parameter is a single value of a statistic

An  estimator  is a statistic (random variable) while an estimate is a value of the estimator.

Goal of an estimation problem: Find a "good" estimator which estimates the population parameter accurately.

## "Good" Estimators {#slide-6}

Are unbiased (on average, equal to their population version)

Precise (small standard errors)

## Example 7 {#slide-41}

Shards of clay vessels were put together to reconstruct rim diameters of the original ceramic vessels found at the Wind Monument archeological site.  A random sample of the ceramic vessels gave the following rim diameters (in cm):

	15.9	13.4	22.1	12.7	13.1	19.6	11.7	13.5	17.7	18.1

Find a 90% confidence interval for the population mean of the rim diameters using the applet. (click enter raw data)

## One sided confidence intervals {#slide-43}

## Introduction {#slide-44}

In some cases, it will be more important to know only either lower bound or upper bound for the parameter.

For example:

If the measurement of interest is tensile strength, the engineer receives better information from a lower bound only. This bound communicates the worst-case scenario.

Inferences need to be made concerning the mean mercury composition in a river. An upper bound is very informative in this case.

## Example 8 {#slide-47}

To estimate the mean life of its machines, a company samples 16 machines and finds that the sample mean is 299.2 and the standard deviation is 80 hours. Assume the mean life of machines is normally distributed. Could the company advertise "their machines last at least 250 hours" with 95% confidence?

## Example 11 {#slide-60}

In a random sample of 500 families owning television sets in the city of Lincoln, it is found that 340 subscribe to HBO. Find a 95% confidence interval for the actual proportion of families with television sets in this city that subscribe to HBO.

## Confidence interval  for the difference of two proportions {#slide-62}

## Example 12 {#slide-63}

A certain change in a process for manufacturing component parts is being considered. Samples are taken under both the existing and the new process so as to determine if the new process results in an improvement.

75 of 1500 items from the existing process are found to be defective.

80 of 2000 items from the new process are found to be defective.

Find a 90% confidence interval for the true difference in the proportion of defectives between the existing and the new process.
